solution: The coefficient of $x^2$ is 1, so each bracket starts with $x$. We need two numbers that multiply to give ${=c}$ (the coefficient of $y^2$) and add to give ${=b}$ (the coefficient of $xy$).
Each number goes with $y$ in its own bracket: $x^2+{=b}xy+{=c}y^2=(x+{=p}y)(x+{=q}y)$.
notes: Basic entry point of the objective: a trinomial in two variables with leading coefficient 1 and all-positive terms, x^2 + bxy + cy^2, the same two-bracket method as the single-variable case with y carried through. The book's nearest questions are ex1-11-30p (x^2-2xy-15y^2, page 39) and ex1-8-19 (a^2-7ab+12b^2, page 27, whose printed stem drops the square on the last b, though its solution has it); this family is the easier, all-positive sibling of those, so signs are not varied here. Parameters: p in 2..5 and q in p+1..9, so p < q, the two factors are always different (no perfect squares, which would invite the (x+py)^2 form and a marker mismatch), and the b and c coefficients are always at least 3 and 6, so no instance prints 1y^2 or a bare 1 coefficient. The answer is symmetric in the two brackets and the marker is declared factorised, so either bracket order should be accepted. Largest instance is x^2+14xy+45y^2. The catalogue holds no misconceptions for this objective and the family is not mcq, so none are used or proposed. Only the basic gap was listed; standard and advanced are already covered by the book questions (signed two-variable, x^4 quadratics, repeated-bracket and bracketed-expression cases), so no further families were written.
